name: Shaving brush

lead: A shaving brush builds lather from soap or cream and spreads it over the beard. The payoff, according to reference works, is a richer lather, lifted hairs and light exfoliation for a smoother, closer shave. Bristles come from badger, boar, horse or synthetic fibre, with silvertip badger the premium grade.
Bristles hold water and whip soap into foam, then lift hairs while spreading lather across the skin. No clinical study of these effects was found.

paras: People soak the brush, load it with soap or cream, and work the lather on the face in circles before shaving. Natural and synthetic brushes are rinsed and dried between uses.

A 2018 historical review describes anthrax outbreaks between 1915 and 1924 from contaminated imported brushes, with about 20 percent mortality; horse hair brushes then fell out of use for about a century.

angle.text: Wet shavers use a brush to build lather and apply it, with reference works crediting it with richer lather, lifted hairs and light exfoliation for a closer shave. The result is visible straight away.

lead: A shaving brush is a handle with a tuft of bristles used to whip shaving soap or cream into lather with water and apply it to the face before shaving.[1][2] Bristles are made from badger, boar, horse hair or synthetic fibre, and graded badger hair is the most prized material.[1]

Wikipedia and Grokipedia say a brush holds water to make a richer lather, lifts facial hairs so that less razor pressure is needed, and gives mild exfoliation.[1][2] No clinical study of these effects on skin or shaving outcomes was found.
The best-documented health episode is historical: between roughly 1915 and 1924, anthrax outbreaks were traced to shaving brushes made with contaminated animal hair.[3]

Wet shaving with soap or cream

paras: Badger grades run from pure, which is coarser and cheaper, through best and super, to silvertip, the rarest and most expensive, with natural white tips that hold much water.[1] Boar bristle is inexpensive and needs soaking before use; synthetic brushes, usually nylon, dry faster and lather with little product; and horse hair has been returning after nearly a century.[1] Grokipedia describes second- and third-generation synthetics from the 2000s and 2010s that imitate the tapered tips of badger hair.[2]

The modern brush is traced to 1750s France, where it was called a blaireau, meaning badger.[1] A Dutch painting of 1648 is the earliest cited image of one, according to Grokipedia.[2] After folding straight razors made home shaving practical in the 1800s, the brush became a status symbol.[1]

Horse hair brushes fell out of use for close to a century after an anthrax scare around the First World War.[1] In 2018 Procter and Gamble stopped using badger hair in its Art of Shaving products after an animal-rights investigation of Chinese suppliers.[1]
No studies found of shaving brushes for skin or appearance outcomes. Historical medical literature documents anthrax cases from contaminated brushes, described below.

A 2018 historical review describes outbreaks of Bacillus anthracis from 1915 to 1924 caused by brushes imported into Europe and the United States from Japan, China and Russia. Makers cut costs by moving from badger to horse and other animal hair, and wartime changes to trade routes and deficient sterilisation were followed by outbreaks in which roughly a fifth of cases were fatal.[3] Case reports published in 1916 and 1920 describe anthrax linked to shaving brushes, including a facial case with recovery.[4][5] Current brushes are not described in these sources as an anthrax risk.
No looksmaxxing forum material specific to shaving brushes was found; mentions in general fitness forums are incidental.

timeline.event: The modern shaving brush appears in France.[1]
